body.p: Claims 1-17 and 19-20 are pending in the present application. Claims 1 is amended in this paper. Claim 19 is canceled in this paper. No new claims are added in this paper.
In taking the foregoing actions, Applicant respectfully submits Applicant is not

necessarily conceding in this application that these claims, as originally presented, are not patentable over the references cited by the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO), as pertinent ones of the present claim amendments and cancellations are only for facilitating expeditious prosecution. Applicant respectfully reserves the right to pursue the canceled claims and/or other claims in one or more continuing applications.
Request for Continued Examination under 37 C.F.R 4 1.114
Concurrently with this response, Applicant has filed a Request for Continued
Examination with the appropriate fee. Applicant respectfully request that prosecution be reopened and all prior rejections be withdrawn.
Claims 1-17 and 19-20 were rejected pursuant to 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) as allegedly

indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor regards as his invention. Specifically the Examiner states "claim 1 recites the limitation "a fuel tank that provides structural support to an airframe of the aircraft and carries shear loads from the airframe". It is unclear how the tank provides structural support or carries shear loads from the airframe". (Office Action, p. 2).
Without conceding the propriety of the rejection, and in the interests of advancing

prosecution, amendments presented in this paper have removed the alleged indefinite language for claim 1. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully submits that this rejection is now moot, and respectfully requests that this rejection of claims 1-17 and 19-20 under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) be withdrawn.
Accordingly, Applicant respectfully requests that all rejections of claims pursuant to 35 U.S.C. § 112 be removed.
Epstein/Clark/Struzik/Glaser
Claims 1, 6-11, 13-17 and 20 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly

unpatentable over US 20150344143 Al to Epstein; Michael Jay et al. (hereinafter "Epstein"), in view of US 6422514 Bl to Clark; William James et al. (hereinafter "Clark") in view of US 20130197791 Al to Struzik; Anthony (hereinafter "Struzik"), and further in view of US 20110042520 Al to Glaser; Daniel et al. (hereinafter "Glaser") (Office Action, p. 3). Applicant respectfully traverses the rejection.
Claim las amended recites:
A method for fueling and using an aircraft, wherein the method comprises:
storing, using a fuel tank comprising a chamber between an inner wall and an outer wall
of the fuel tank, wherein the chamber is configured to insulate a liquid gas fuel by
prevention of condensation of humidity within the fuel tank of the aircraft;
fueling, using a fuel line, the aircraft, wherein fueling further comprises:

filling the fuel tank with liquified gas fuel to a desired level, wherein the desired level comprises fuel for a plurality of flights plus reserves, wherein a sensor connected to the fuel tank detects at least abnormal phenomena related insulation of the fuel tank, wherein the sensor is configured to detect humidity within the fuel tank; and convert the detected at least abnormal phenomena into a signal that is then transmitted to a computing device; and removing, using the computing device, the fuel line as function of the desired level in the aircraft; and
preparing the fuel tank for flight as a function of the desired level; and flying, using the aircraft, a plurality of flights using the liquid gas fuel.

The Office states that Epstein does not disclose "wherein a sensor connected to the fuel tank detects at least abnormal phenomena related to the fuel tank, wherein the sensor converts the detected at least abnormal phenomena into a signal that is then transmitted to a computing device." (Office Action, p. 4). The Office has not asserted that Clark nor Struzik disclose "wherein a sensor connected to the fuel tank detects at least abnormal phenomena related to the fuel tank, wherein the sensor converts the detected at least abnormal phenomena into a signal that is then transmitted to a computing device," as previously disclosed in claim 1. As such, Applicant respectfully submits that claim 1 is patentably distinguishable over Epstein, Clark, and Struzik, alone or in combination, for at least the reasons discussed above.

The Office asserts that Glaser discloses "wherein a sensor connected to the fuel tank detects at least abnormal phenomena related to the fuel tank, wherein the sensor converts the detected at least abnormal phenomena into a signal that is then transmitted to a computing device" citing paragraph 0015 of Glaser stating, in part:
The control device configured for example in the form of an electronic control device
controls the shut-off valve preferably on the basis of sensor signals that indicate whether
the exhaust air outlet connection connected to the aeration- and/or deaeration device of the aircraft tank system is connected to the aeration- and/or deaeration connection of the
storage tank of the refueling unit. The control device controls the shut-off valve into a
dosed position only if the sensor signals indicate to the control device that there is a
proper connection of the exhaust air outlet connection of the tank system to the aeration- and/or deaeration connection of the storage tank of the refueling unit.

However, Applicant asserts Glaser does not teach, suggest, or motivate "wherein the sensor is configured to detect humidity within the fuel tank; and convert the detected at least abnormal phenomena into a signal that is then transmitted to a computing device," wherein the fuel tank comprises "a chamber between an inner wall and an outer wall of the fuel tank, wherein the chamber is configured to insulate a liquid gas fuel by prevention of condensation of humidity within the fuel tank of the aircraft," as disclosed in amended claim 1. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully submits that claim 1 as amended is patentably distinguishable over Epstein, Clark, Struzik, and Glaser, alone or in combination, for at least the reasons discussed above. Therefore, Applicant respectfully requests the withdrawal of this rejection. Claims 6-11, 13-17 and 20

Each of claims 6-11, 13-17 and 20 depends, directly or indirectly, from claim 1. As noted above, claim 3 is patentably distinguishable over Epstein, Clark, Struzik, and Glaser, alone or in combination, for at least the reasons discussed above. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully submits that claims 6-11, 13-17 and 20 are patentably distinguishable over Epstein, Clark, Struzik, and Glaser, alone or in combination, for at least the reasons discussed above. Therefore, Applicant respectfully requests the withdrawal of these rejections.
Epstein/Clark/Struzik/Glaser/D'Auvergne
Claim 2 stands rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly unpatentable Epstein, Clark, Struzik and Glaser as applied to claims above, and further in view of US 7281682 B2
D'Auvergne; Hector A. (hereinafter "D'Auvergne") (Office Action, p. 7). Applicant respectfully traverses the rejection.

Claim 2 depends directly from claim 1. As noted above, claim 1 as amended is patentably distinguishable over Epstein, Clark, Struzik, and Glaser, alone or in combination, for at least the reasons discussed above. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully submits that claim 2 is patentably distinguishable over Epstein, Clark, Struzik, and Glaser, alone or in combination, for at least the reasons discussed above.

D'Auvergne fails to cure the deficiencies of Epstein, Clark, Struzik, and Glaser. The Office has not asserted that D'Auvergne discloses "wherein the sensor is configured to detect humidity within the fuel tank; and convert the detected at least abnormal phenomena into a signal that is then transmitted to a computing device," wherein the fuel tank comprises "a chamber between an inner wall and an outer wall of the fuel tank, wherein the chamber is configured to insulate a liquid gas fuel by prevention of condensation of humidity within the fuel tank of the aircraft," as disclosed in amended claim 1. Applicant asserts D'Auvergne does not teach, suggest, or motivate "wherein the sensor is configured to detect humidity within the fuel tank; convert the detected at least abnormal phenomena into a signal that is then transmitted to a computing device," wherein the fuel tank comprises "a chamber between an inner wall and an outer wall of the fuel tank, wherein the chamber is configured to insulate a liquid gas fuel by prevention of condensation of humidity within the fuel tank of the aircraft," as disclosed in amended claim 1. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully submits that claim 2 is patentably distinguishable over Epstein, Clark, Struzik, Glaser, and D'Auvergne, alone or in combination, for at least the reasons discussed above. Therefore, Applicant respectfully requests the withdrawal of this rejection.
Epstein/Glaser/Wexler/Connor

Claims 3-5, and 19 stands rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly unpatentable over Epstein and Glaser as applied to claims above, in view of US 6123295 Al Wexler; Mark Harry et al. (hereinafter "Wexler") and further in view of NPL "What is Aerogel" by Nick Connor (hereinafter "Conner"). (Office Action, p. 7). Applicant respectfully traverses the rejection.

Claim 19 is canceled in this paper, rendering rejection under 103 now moot. Each of claims 3-5 depends from claim 1. As noted above, claim 1 as amended is patentably distinguishable over Epstein and Glaser, alone or in combination, for at least the reasons discussed above. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully submits that claims 3-5 are patentably distinguishable over Epstein and Glaser, alone or in combination, for at least the reasons discussed above.

Wexler and Connor fail to cure the deficiencies of Epstein and Glaser. The Office has not asserted that Wexler or Conor disclose "wherein the sensor is configured to detect humidity within the fuel tank; and convert the detected at least abnormal phenomena into a signal that is then transmitted to a computing device," wherein the fuel tank comprises "a chamber between an inner wall and an outer wall of the fuel tank, wherein the chamber is configured to insulate a liquid gas fuel by prevention of condensation of humidity within the fuel tank of the aircraft," as disclosed in amended claim 1. Applicant asserts Wexler and Connor do not teach, suggest, or motivate "wherein the sensor is configured to detect humidity within the fuel tank; and convert the detected at least abnormal phenomena into a signal that is then transmitted to a computing device," wherein the fuel tank comprises "a chamber between an inner wall and an outer wall of the fuel tank, wherein the chamber is configured to insulate a liquid gas fuel by prevention of condensation of humidity within the fuel tank of the aircraft," as disclosed in amended claim 1. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully submits that claims 3-5 are patentably distinguishable over Epstein, Glaser, Wexler, and Connor, alone or in combination, for at least the reasons discussed above. Therefore, Applicant respectfully requests the withdrawal of these rejections.
Epstein/Clark/Struzik/Glaser/Benassi

Claim 12 stands rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly unpatentable Epstein, Clark, Struzik and Glaser as applied to claims above, and further in view of US 20120119032 Al Benassi; Eric et al. (Office Action, p. 8). Applicant respectfully traverses the rejection.
Claim 12 depends from claim 1. As noted above, claim 1 as amended is patentably
distinguishable over Epstein, Clark, Struzik, and Glaser, alone or in combination, for at least the reasons discussed above. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully submits that claim 12 is patentably
distinguishable over Epstein, Clark, Struzik, and Glaser, alone or in combination, for at least the reasons discussed above.

Benassi fails to cure the deficiencies of Epstein, Clark, Struzik, and Glaser. The Office has not asserted that Benassi discloses "wherein the sensor is configured to detect humidity within the fuel tank; and convert the detected at least abnormal phenomena into a signal that is then transmitted to a computing device," wherein the fuel tank comprises "a chamber between an inner wall and an outer wall of the fuel tank, wherein the chamber is configured to insulate a liquid gas fuel by prevention of condensation of humidity within the fuel tank of the aircraft," as disclosed in amended claim 1. Applicant asserts Benassi does not teach, suggest, or motivate "wherein the sensor is configured to detect humidity within the fuel tank; and convert the detected at least abnormal phenomena into a signal that is then transmitted to a computing device," wherein the fuel tank comprises "a chamber between an inner wall and an outer wall of the fuel tank, wherein the chamber is configured to insulate a liquid gas fuel by prevention of condensation of humidity within the fuel tank of the aircraft," as disclosed in amended claim 1. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully submits that claim 12 is patentably distinguishable over Epstein, Clark, Struzik, Glaser, and Benassi, alone or in combination, for at least the reasons discussed above. Therefore, Applicant respectfully requests the withdrawal of this rejection.
Accordingly, Applicant respectfully submits that all claims in the application are in a

condition for allowance and respectfully solicit the prompt issuance of a Notice of Allowance. If any issues remain, the Examiner is encouraged to call the undersigned practitioner at the number listed below.
Respectfully submitted, /Princess Onwuzuligbo/
